name: Daridorexant

lead: Daridorexant (Quviviq) is a prescription sleep medicine for adults with insomnia. People interested in looks follow it because deeper, longer sleep is linked with clearer skin, less puffiness and a fresher face.

It works by blocking orexin receptors OX1R and OX2R, which turns down the brain's wake signal rather than boosting GABA. Two phase 3 trials examined night-time and daytime insomnia symptoms; appearance has not been a studied outcome.

paras: It is taken as a prescribed nightly tablet by adults diagnosed with insomnia, usually as part of a broader sleep routine. People who use it for recovery describe the aim as more consistent sleep, with any change in skin or facial freshness following over weeks of better rest.

Reported effects include sleepiness and headache. The label warns about next-day impairment, sleep paralysis, complex sleep behaviors and mood effects. It is prescription-only and a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Daridorexant is a prescription orexin-blocking sleep drug (Quviviq). The idea is deeper, longer sleep leading to better overnight recovery, which shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It has been studied in insomnia trials.

lead: Daridorexant, sold as Quviviq, is a prescription dual orexin receptor antagonist for adults with insomnia involving difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep. It was developed by Idorsia Pharmaceuticals and was formerly known as nemorexant during development.[1]

Wikipedia reports US FDA approval in January 2022 (available from May 2022, Schedule IV) and EU authorisation in April 2022, with UK and Canadian approvals in 2023.[2] Grokipedia gives the dates as 7 January and 29 April 2022 and describes it as the third orexin receptor antagonist approved for insomnia after suvorexant and lemborexant.[1][3] Two phase 3 trials examined both night-time and daytime symptoms of insomnia.[4]

It has no approved or studied appearance indication. The link people draw to looks runs through sleep: better sleep and recovery are discussed as supporting skin, energy and training. Reported adverse effects include somnolence and headache, and the label warns of next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors.[5]

paras: The route from daridorexant to appearance is entirely through sleep. People who work on how they look commonly treat sleep as the foundation of recovery after training, of energy and mood, and of a rested face with less puffiness and fewer dark circles. Insomnia that is long-standing and distressing is the condition for which daridorexant is prescribed, and the aim of treatment in trials is shorter time to fall asleep, less waking during the night and better daytime functioning.[4][5]

Drug treatment is one of several options in insomnia care. The European Insomnia Guideline 2023 update places cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia as first-line treatment and describes orexin antagonists among the medicines that may be considered when it is unavailable or insufficient.[6]

The label indicates daridorexant for adults with insomnia characterised by difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance.[5] European guidelines discuss orexin antagonists among the pharmacological options for insomnia.[6] No cosmetic or appearance use is approved or has been studied.

Daridorexant blocks both orexin receptors, OX1R and OX2R, reducing the wake-promoting effect of orexin neuropeptides made in the hypothalamus.[5][1] This differs from benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, which act on GABA-A receptors.[1] It is primarily metabolised by CYP3A4, and the label addresses use with CYP3A4 inhibitors and in hepatic impairment.[5][1]

Wikipedia describes daridorexant as blocking both OX1 and OX2 orexin receptors with roughly equal potency; orexins promote wakefulness, and the sleep-promoting effect is thought to come mainly from OX2 blockade. It does not act on GABA receptors, unlike benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.[2] Oral bioavailability is about 62%, peak levels occur in 1 to 2 hours, it is mostly metabolised by CYP3A4, and its half-life is about 8 hours.[2]

Orexin (hypocretin) neuropeptides made in the hypothalamus promote wakefulness through the OX1 and OX2 receptors. Dual antagonists such as daridorexant block both, whereas selective antagonists block only one.[7] Wikipedia lists the orexin antagonists approved for insomnia as suvorexant (Belsomra, August 2014), lemborexant (Dayvigo, December 2019) and daridorexant (Quviviq, January 2022), with further agents approved later in Japan and China.[7]

Grokipedia lists somnolence and headache as common effects and notes rarer risks including complex sleep behaviors, sleep paralysis, hallucinations and next-day impairment.[1] The label includes warnings on CNS-depressant effects, sleep paralysis and cataplexy-like symptoms, complex sleep behaviors, respiratory function and worsening depression or suicidal ideation, and the drug is Schedule IV in the US.[5][1]

Wikipedia lists headache, somnolence or fatigue, dizziness and nausea as common, mostly at rates similar to placebo, notes possible next-morning driving impairment, and reports no rebound insomnia or withdrawal in trials. It is contraindicated in narcolepsy and should not be combined with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.[2]

For the orexin-antagonist class, Wikipedia reports that somnolence or fatigue occurred in about 5 to 10 percent of trial participants depending on drug and dose, compared with roughly 1 to 4 percent on placebo, and that narcolepsy, a condition of orexin deficiency, is a contraindication.[7]

Two multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials at 156 sites in 17 countries assessed safety and efficacy on night-time and daytime insomnia symptoms.[4] A separate trial studied older adults with insomnia disorder, and a long-term study reported safety and tolerability data.[8][9] A narrative review describes the drug's pharmacology and trial programme.[10] Grokipedia summarises trials as showing reductions in wake after sleep onset and increases in total sleep time versus placebo.[1]

Network meta-analyses and guidelines place orexin antagonists among treatment options for insomnia, with comparisons across drug classes.[11][6] Registered studies include trials in people with insomnia and nocturia and a dose-finding study in adolescents.[12][13] No studies have examined appearance outcomes.

According to Wikipedia's summary of the phase 3 programme, 25 to 50 mg shortened time to persistent sleep by roughly 6 to 12 minutes versus placebo, reduced wake after sleep onset by about 10 to 23 minutes and increased subjective total sleep time by about 10 to 22 minutes, with daytime functioning improving at the higher dose. A 2022 network meta-analysis reported a small effect size versus placebo (standardised mean difference 0.23), smaller than for suvorexant and lemborexant and for benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.[2][11] Treatment for up to a year was generally well tolerated in long-term data.[9][2]

The phase 3 programme was designed with polysomnography primary endpoints, wake time after sleep onset and latency to persistent sleep at months 1 and 3, plus secondary endpoints for self-reported total sleep time and a daytime sleepiness score. In study 1 participants received 50 mg, 25 mg or placebo each evening for three months and in study 2 25 mg, 10 mg or placebo.[4]

A 2025 network meta-analysis of eight placebo-controlled trials covering 5,198 adults compared daridorexant, lemborexant and suvorexant on sleep onset, total sleep time, wake after sleep onset, Insomnia Severity Index scores, discontinuation and adverse events, and reported that all active treatments outperformed placebo on at least some measures.[14] A multicentre phase 3 trial in China enrolled adults aged 18 to 75 with DSM-5 insomnia disorder and a baseline Insomnia Severity Index of at least 15.[15]

Daridorexant originated at Actelion Pharmaceuticals and was developed further by Idorsia; it was patented in 2013 and first described in the scientific literature in 2017, according to Wikipedia.[2] It was known as nemorexant during development.[1]
Daridorexant is marketed as Quviviq in several countries.[1] It does not feature prominently in looksmaxxing communities.
It is a prescription-only medicine in the US (Schedule IV), UK, EU and Canada.[2] It was the first orexin receptor antagonist available in the EU.[2]
